transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Alex (Redwood SE), Priya (Solutions Eng), Noah (CSM); Maya (Aurelia ML), Jordan (Platform), Liam (CTO), Sofia (SRE), Devon (Data)

Summary:
Quick sync on the week-to-week POC results. We saw TTFT oscillations when microburst traffic hit the streaming path; sequence length distribution from Aurelia moved the kernel choice threshold; discussed hedging and fallback to compact quantized variants. Agreed next steps to run targeted microburst hedging and share traffic samples.

Topics covered:
- First token time (TTFT) and streaming jitter
- Sequence length distribution impact on kernel selection
- Microburst hedging config and priority queues
- Quantization vs accuracy tradeoffs for 8-bit fast kernels
- Security / KMS question list for private deployment evaluation

Action items (recorded in notes): see metadata action_items

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick roll call?
[00:05] Maya: Maya here.
[00:06] Jordan: Jordan. we have Sofia and Devon as well.
[00:08] Liam: Liam on.
[00:10] Alex: Alex from Redwood, hi. Priya and Noah here too.
[00:15] Samir: Cool. agenda for today is to go through the numbers Alex pulled from last week's run, talk microburst impact, and decide the experiment matrix for the hedging tests. any additional items?
[00:25] Sophia: (sic) Sofia - small security Q at the end about KMS and key rotation.
[00:28] Samir: Yup we'll leave time. Alex do you want to kick off with the findings?
[00:30] Alex: Yeah. so quick context — we replayed your traffic sample from Tue and Fri, and we instrumented TTFT at the front of the stream and per-chunk latencies. what we saw — higher variance in TTFT when there were sustained microbursts > 120 concurrent streams. baseline kernel A (fast matmul) wins for short sequences but when seq len went above ~420 the runtime switched to kernel B and that switch is what's causing a 35-120ms step increase in first-token latency.
[01:05] Devon: can you clarify "switch" — is that an automatic kernel swap at runtime?
[01:08] Alex: yes it's a runtime decision based on seqlen and batch shape. sometimes it's per-request heuristics, sometimes precompiled. we do have a hedging path where a slow kernel is started in parallel for long seq when we expect jitter, but that increases GPU cycles.
[01:25] Jordan: With hedging what's the typical overhead? curious about cost delta.
[01:28] Priya: Overhead varies; our microburst hedging config adds roughly 12-18% GPU time in this workload but reduces tail TTFT by 40-60% for those events. again depends on quant and batch packing.
[01:45] Maya: quick interjection — our production seq length median is around 180 but 95th is 640, because of a small set of long documents and some streaming chats that include full context.
[01:58] Alex: that distribution explains the oscillation: most requests use kernel A, occasional long ones force kernel B and the runtime cache/kv cache state flush causes the microburst to impact others. also small misc transcription note: sometimes KV cache got logged as "k v cache" in the pipeline, sorry for the confusion in the sheet.
[02:20] Samir: important — we need to decide whether to bias the runtime to prefer kernel A plus quantized slower path for long seq, or accept the kernel swap and hedge. tradeoffs?
[02:30] Alex: Option 1: prefer kernel A — do more aggressive sequence chunking/early output to keep seqlen perceived small. pros: TTFT for most wins. cons: may degrade long-seq quality and increases prefix overhead. Option 2: keep kernel B for correctness and use hedging to protect TTFT during bursts. pros: maintains quality; cons: more GPU cost. Option 3: force quantized kernel-A-like execution for long seq — needs eval on quality drop.
[02:58] Jordan: do we have an eval on quantized answers for our use-case? recall last time some medical Q-A had hallucination edgecases.
[03:05] Alex: we ran a small eval against your prompt set — 8-bit dynamic quant showed a 2.7% drop in ROUGE-like metric on the clinical QA subset, with occasional token-level differences. We can expand that test.
[03:22] Maya: Ok we can't accept anything that risks hallucinating clinical advice. accuracy is hard requirement.
[03:28] Priya: understood. then hedging looks preferable as a first step, but we should optimize hedging to be cheaper: e.g., microburst windowing, only hedge requests when the server sees > N in 100ms, and cancel speculative kernels if early tokens come back.
[03:45] Samir: that aligns with our suggestion of adaptive hedging. Alex, what config did you try?
[03:50] Alex: tried naively: hedge all sequences predicted to be long; that was costly. second run: only hedge when concurrent streams > 80 and predicted seqlen > 400 — that dropped overhead to ~11% and saved 70% of tail TTFT incidents. We can make the threshold dynamic.
[04:12] Liam: curious — how deterministic is the runtime decision? does it flip-flop mid-request?
[04:16] Alex: good question. the flip happens at model compile boundaries and sometimes mid-request when we re-evaluate kv cache shape; it's not ideal. making it deterministic per-request is part of our kernel decision workstream (link: confluence/kernel-decisions-2027).
[04:35] Jordan: any quick wins for sequence-length normalization on our side?
[04:38] Devon: we could truncate older context for streaming chat or snapshot only last N tokens, but we worry about losing context for follow-ups. maybe summarization as a pre-step?
[04:49] Maya: summarization would change semantics of some clinical workflows. If we do it, it must be reversible or clearly flagged.
[04:55] Alex: another middle ground: server-side prefix caching — avoid sending full prefix each time. that helps with KV cache churn.
[05:03] Priya: and batching heuristics — continuous batching with priority lanes: short requests in fast lane, long ones in slow lane. We sketched a priority queue in the last workshop.
[05:14] Samir: let's step through the numbers in the sheet — Samir shares: latency_results_may12.xlsx (link in chat)
[05:20] Alex: row highlight 12-21: baseline median TTFT 78ms; tail 99th 420ms during microburst. hedging config reduces 99th to 180ms but bump in GPU utilization.
[05:35] Jordan: can we simulate cost at scale? like projected monthly GPU hours delta?
[05:38] Alex: we estimated a 14% increase in GPU hours for the hedging profile, which translates to a projected $Xk/mo on dedicated pool; Samir will attach pricing delta.
[05:50] Sofia: quick security note — if we move to private deployment we need KMS integration and audit logs; we also have to confirm if the hedging logs keep token-level info.
[06:02] Noah: we redact tokens in logs by default; but we can enable structured trace with hashes only for troubleshooting. we'll follow up with a security doc.
[06:10] Maya: excellent. back to experiments: what's the plan for next week?
[06:14] Alex: propose two parallel experiments: (A) microburst hedging with dynamic threshold and early cancel; (B) sequence normalization via light summarization for tail requests (non-production prompts only). We'll run both on replayed traffic and measure TTFT, token accuracy for clinical subset, and GPU hours.
[06:34] Samir: good. which one do you recommend we do first?
[06:36] Alex: hedging first, since it doesn't touch model outputs. summarization second after we validate semantics.
[06:42] Priya: also include a compile-time kernel preference test: force kernel-A path for a small subset to measure accuracy delta. low risk if run on canary.
[06:49] Liam: can we do a 5% canary of real traffic in staging to validate hedging without affecting prod?
[06:54] Alex: yes. need traffic sample and gating rules; Jordan and Maya to provide gating.
[06:59] Jordan: we can provide anonymized traffic and a route in staging. we'll also include 5% user segment that is non-critical.
[07:07] Samir: timeline?
[07:09] Alex: start hedging run Wednesday with replay traces then move to canary Friday; report back next Tuesday (2027-05-19).
[07:18] Maya: sounds good. what metrics to include in the report?
[07:20] Alex: median and 95/99 TTFT, per-chunk latency, quality eval on the clinical prompt set (ROUGE/EM proxies), GPU hours delta, and a simple cost projection.
[07:33] Samir: also include logs of kernel-switch events and KV cache eviction counts.
[07:38] Devon: for the replay we can feed the anonymized traces; will there be any postprocessing we need to do?
[07:42] Alex: we need the trace in our replay format; Maya said earlier they could export in JSON with timestamps. otherwise we can do a quick conversion.
[07:50] Priya: security follow-up — we'll put together a short KMS and SOC2 checklist and send it to Sofia. Samir: you'll include the security pack in the shared folder?
[07:58] Samir: yes I'll upload security_pack_aurelia.zip along with the latency sheet and the confluence link.
[08:04] Sofia: perfect. also please note we need encryption-at-rest confirmation for logs.
[08:08] Noah: confirmed — default logs are encrypted; we'll note rotation policy.
[08:12] Alex: quick FYI — there's slight transcription artifacts we left in the sheet: model names like "spectrahealth" got conflated; ignore those.
[08:20] Maya: any competitor angle we should be aware of — Jordan asked earlier about Vertex/managed endpoints?
[08:24] Samir: we saw some baseline comparisons; competitors can do managed endpoints but don't offer the adaptive hedging and kernel-level control we provide. will capture that in a short note.
[08:34] Liam: last thing — on the pricing side, if we go hedging+dedicated, is there a committed discount tier we can discuss?
[08:39] Samir: yes that's a commercial discussion; once you pick a target commitment we can model savings. I'll attach preliminary ranges in the sheet.
[08:47] Jordan: ok good. to recap next steps: Samir share artifacts, Alex run hedging experiments, Maya/Jordan provide traces, Priya prepare kernel tradeoff slides, Sofia get security Qs.
[08:58] Samir: perfect. any final questions?
[09:01] Maya: none. thanks all.
[09:04] Liam: thanks.
[09:06] Alex: thanks everyone.
[09:10] Samir: we'll reconvene next Tuesday for results. end.
